canberra.title: Government wants to offload heritage-listed Woden landmark, eyes adaptive reuse
canberra.snippet: The space-age looking, heritage-listed Callam Offices in Woden that the ACT Government is looking to sell would be best used as something...
canberra.content:
Callam Offices has been empty since mid-2025 and needs lots of work. Photo: John Coleman.

The space-age looking, heritage-listed Callam Offices in Woden that the ACT Government is looking to sell would be best used as something other than offices, given the amount of vacant space in the Town Centre and the cost of bringing the building up to scratch, a Legislative Assembly committee hearing was told on Thursday.

The committee also heard that while the heritage listing imposed considerable constraints on what could be done with the building, compromise was possible to enable an adaptive reuse proposal.

The Standing Committee on Environment, Planning, Transport and City Services was conducting a public hearing for its Inquiry into the Role and Future of the Woden Town Centre.

The unusual, architecturally significant three-pod complex was built for $9 million between 1977 and 1981, when it was handed over to the Woden TAFE College, but it has been empty since mid-2025.

It is now in the hands of Infrastructure Canberra and the Suburban Land Agency, and the ACT Government wants to sell the building and surrounding land (Section 80 Phillip) for redevelopment, due to the prohibitive cost of maintaining and refurbishing it.

The government has been advised it would cost $128 million to make it fit for reoccupation as offices. The 2026-27 ACT Budget allocated $1.782 million over two years for essential maintenance and operations.

Committee member Independent Fiona Carrick would like to see the building used for community purposes such as arts and cultural facilities, indoor sports, children’s and family services, youth programs and housing community organisations.

She wanted to know what plans the SLA had for the building.

SLA official Irena Sharp told the hearing the agency was assessing whether the site could form part of the land release identified for 2027-28.

Ms Carrick asked whether the SLA intended to include Callam Offices in the release and if its current state would be a hindrance to putting it on the market. Ms Sharp said the SLA was looking at a range of options.

“We certainly need to address the future of Callam offices, and land redevelopment and the urban renewal of that area is closely linked to how Callum Offices can function in the future,” she said.

The building has significant redevelopment constraints. Photo: John Coleman.

Ms Sharp said that if the building was earmarked for offices then the $128 million upgrade cost would need to be taken into account.

“That would be the outcome that we would be seeking from the market, and of course that would need to be weighed up against the value of the land,” she said.

“But office use, to be honest, at this point in time, Woden Town Centre shares quite a lot of vacant space in offices, so it’s not necessarily a recommended use of the building, and putting it to the market would actually open up the opportunities to look at what other options and uses could be created for Callam Offices in the context of a future precinct.”

Ms Sharp said the SLA also had to consider what its heritage listing meant when going to market because of additional conservation requirements.

Public Service Minister Rachel Stephen-Smith said the government was not considering pursuing de-listing of the building but indicated that there could be ground given in the case of an adaptive reuse proposal.

She did not think a delisting proposal would be successful “but the Suburban land Agency has been working with the Heritage Council to understand, within the heritage requirements, what is possible”.

“There are some really significant constraints associated with that building, and we certainly know that in terms of adaptive reuse of other heritage buildings in other cities, having some compromise to enable a building to be usable is a good thing.”

Ms Stephen-Smith had previously told Ms Carrick in an answer to a question on notice that a “standalone economic assessment specifically quantifying the benefits of retaining the site for community organisations, arts and culture has not been undertaken”.

Ms Carrick sought, on notice, a complete breakdown of the $128 million cost.

Early last year Infrastructure Canberra Director-General Gillian Geraghty told Ms Carrick that the Callam Offices had a number of compliance issues to do with fire safety and egress, accessibility and lifts, energy efficiency and air quality standards, and modern engineering requirements for structural components.

The Callam Offices were added to the ACT Heritage Register in 2008.

They are one of two large government office commissions in Canberra designed in the 1970s by John Andrews, and designed and detailed in the Late Twentieth-Century Structuralist manner.

canberra.title: Union calls for immediate pause on complex automated decision-making in public service agencies
canberra.snippet: Commonwealth-employed public servants want their agencies to stop making automated decisions until the Federal Government sorts out clear...
canberra.content:
CPSU deputy secretary Rebecca Fawcett says the Federal Government must learn from the mistakes of Robodebt and not rush into automated decision-making. Photo: CPSU.

Commonwealth-employed public servants want their agencies to stop making automated decisions until the Federal Government sorts out clear regulations and safeguards.

A massive 98 per cent of Community and Public Sector Union members who attended a town hall meeting this week voted in favour of an immediate pause to complex automated decision-making processes across the Australian Public Service agencies.

The union is calling on the government to impose an immediate pause on the automated decisions until service-wide rules are put in place.

They are demanding the government develop “clear and mandatory safeguards” for the public service.

Members attending the meeting and voting on the motion were from agencies across the APS, including Services Australia; the National Disability Insurance Agency; Department of Health, Disability and Ageing; Department of Veterans’ Affairs; and the Australian Taxation Office.

Of particular concern is the practice of allowing an algorithm to determine a person’s access to or level of support, with little or no capacity for human intervention.

Members also expressed frustration over the way automated tools can harmfully impact the lives of Australian families.

Transparency was another concern, with more than a third of members saying they were unaware of whether automated decision-making was being used in their agencies.

A recent report by the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner revealed there is limited disclosure in this area across most agencies.

With the tragedies of the illegal Robodebt scheme still fresh in most minds, CPSU deputy secretary Rebecca Fawcett said the government needs to learn from those mistakes as complex automated decision-making processes are rolled out.

“Public sector workers understand better than anyone the risks of rolling out complex automated decision-making systems without proper safeguards, transparency and accountability,” she said.

“The lesson from Robodebt is clear – government must not allow complex automated decision-making to operate ahead of clear rules that protect people, uphold public service values and ensure decisions can be properly explained and challenged.

“When frontline workers are consulted and genuinely listened to, governments make better decisions. Workers can identify practical risks and unintended consequences before they become serious problems for the community.

“With public concerns about the algorithmic decision-making in aged care, and a similar assessment tool planned for the NDIS, it is critical that we have clear and mandatory safeguards in place before systems are embedded in ways that could negatively affect the community – Australian families and public sector workers.”

The union said it will continue to advocate for transparency, accountability and common sense in automated decision-making in public services, including the need for stronger protections around artificial intelligence in the current round of APS service-wide bargaining.

Under new Privacy Act obligations, APS agencies must start disclosing when computer programs help decide people’s rights and entitlements.

At the same time, all agencies are being told to build and use more such programs through the government’s new AI platform and training mandate called GovAI.

The platform includes a catalogue of AI tools, hands-on training, and a secure sandbox where APS staff can test AI processes. It will also help teams to share and collaborate across agencies.

In launching GovAI recently, Public Service Minister Katy Gallagher said it was designed to empower public servants to develop AI skills in a “safe and ethical” way, as the government looks to integrate more AI solutions into everyday work.

“AI is increasingly becoming a feature of modern workplaces across Australia and the world, which is why the public service must be capable of harnessing the opportunities it provides while also maintaining public trust,” Senator Gallagher said.

“A safe and methodical adoption plan for the uptake of AI in the APS will mean better outcomes for public servants, for Australians who rely on everyday services, and for Australian companies doing business with the Commonwealth.”

canberra.title: Monaro man allegedly threatens to kill federal MP on social media
canberra.snippet: Police have charged a 53-year-old man after he allegedly threatened to kill a federal MP. An Australian Federal Police (AFP) spokesperson...
canberra.content:
3 September 2026

A 53-year-old from Berridale has been arrested after allegedly trying to kill a federal parliamentarian. Photo: John Lomnicki.

Police have charged a 53-year-old man after he allegedly threatened to kill a federal MP.

An Australian Federal Police (AFP) spokesperson said their National Security Investigations (NSI) team began an investigation in July 2026 after receiving a report of an alleged online threat to kill a federal parliamentarian.

Police allegedly linked a man from the NSW town of Berridale to the offending social media post.

They raided his home, seizing a mobile phone for examination, and charged him with one count of using a carriage service to make a threat to kill.

This charge carries a maximum penalty of 10 years’ jail.

The man faced the NSW Local Courts on Thursday (3 September), where he was granted bail on conditions including that he not go near Parliament House, not enter the Sydney suburb of Redfern, not contact the MP and not use any social media platform.

His matter was adjourned to the Queanbeyan Local Court on 15 September.

AFP Commissioner Krissy Barrett announced the establishment of NSI teams last year to target groups and individuals causing high levels of harm to Australia’s social cohesion, including targeting federal parliamentarians.

canberra.title: CIT governance, merger proposal to be probed in new inquiry
canberra.snippet: A new, wide-ranging inquiry has been announced into the troubled Canberra Institute of Technology’s governance arrangements, includ...
canberra.content:
The committee’s CIT governance inquiry will be more expansive than the current review. Photo: Ian Bushnell.

A new, wide-ranging inquiry has been announced into the troubled Canberra Institute of Technology’s governance arrangements, including a potential merger with the University of Canberra.

The separate inquiry by the Legislative Assembly’s Standing Committee on Economics, Recreation and Industry comes despite the ACT Government’s current review of CIT governance, launched in response to the controversy surrounding the recruitment of former CEO Margot McNeill.

CIT has also been the subject of a corruption investigation and findings that led to a previous CEO, Leanne Cover, quitting. It also has budget problems, running regular deficits.

The committee will examine options for improving or reforming governance, including maintaining the CIT Board, reducing the vocational training organisation’s independence from government and the merger proposal championed by UC Vice-Chancellor Bill Shorten.

It will look at ministerial accountability and parliamentary oversight, particularly relating to the use of public funds and the conduct of senior officials; the capability and effectiveness of the board; and the management of conflicts of interest, misconduct and complaints.

Committee chair Taimus Werner-Gibbings said the inquiry was in response to strong community interest and would be broader than the government review.

Mr Taimus-Gibbings said Mr Shorten’s call for CIT to merge with UC also influenced the committee’s decision to launch an inquiry.

He said the committee would have a more expansive remit than what the government was doing, including identifying how long CIT’s problems had been present and whether they were systemic.

“Does it go back 10 years, or 2015 since the board came?” Mr Werner-Gibbings said.

“What are the arguments for and against bringing CIT governance back into a more closely government-managed approach?

“I think we’re going to have a broader investigation and interrogation of the issues now, in the future and previously around CIT and its governance.”

The merger proposal posed opportunities and risks so it made sense to include it, Mr Werner-Gibbings said.

The committee hoped to examine the experience of other dual-sector campuses such as Swinburne University and RMIT in Melbourne.

“What would a merger look like? What are the experiences of other TAFE university mergers like Swinburne and RMIT? Is there a best-practice process that can be followed through? Are there risks to TAFE education in the ACT if that’s undertaken?” Mr Werner-Gibbings said.

He said the committee was seeking submissions from CIT stakeholders, apprentices, skills and trades organisations, and other TAFE organisations in Australia.

“We will cast a very broad net for people who use CIT and rely on CIT and also work in CIT as well, and then go a bit further out of the ACT to other jurisdictions to see how their TAFE system is working,” he said.

Asked whether a new inquiry would revisit issues that the board would rather draw a line under, Mr Taimus-Gibbings said that may be the case, but the committee had an obligation to the people of the ACT and its remit within the Assembly to look at issues that it thought worthwhile airing, discussing, and making recommendations on.

Submissions can be made until the end of October and public hearings will be held in November.

Mr Werner-Gibbings expected a report to be finalised around the first sitting week of 2027.

He said it would be a significant body of work and report for the ACT.

“CIT is really important for the ACT, across the range of people who rely on CIT, who need CIT and want CIT to prosper,” he said.

“Hopefully we’ll be able to make some useful recommendations at the end.”

To learn more, visit the Legislative Assembly.

canberra.title: Teens’ human rights breached by excessive police delays
canberra.snippet: The prosecution of four alleged teenage burglars has been ordered to end after police put the investigation on hold to work on an unrelat...
canberra.content:
ALS Acting CEO Sharif Deen (left) and ACT Human Rights Commissioner Penelope Mathew have welcomed the Childrens Court’s decision. Photos: Supplied, Michelle Kroll, NZLS.

The prosecution of four alleged teenage burglars has been ordered to end after police put the investigation on hold to work on an unrelated attempted murder.

The decision by the ACT Childrens Court’s Magistrate Amy Begley was welcomed by the lawyer for one of the boys, Anastasia Qvist of Fortify Legal.

“The life and liberty of young people, and justice for any victims, should not be put on the back burner until police decide their matters are worthy of investigation,” Ms Qvist said.

According to Magistrate Begley’s recently published decision, the four boys allegedly committed offences over two days in June 2024 when they were aged between 14 and 16.

Their charges included burglary, robbery, assault, participating in a criminal group and driving-related offences.

But it took from October 2025 to February 2026 for them to start facing their charges in court.

Police said the delay in charging the teens arose because the lead investigator became the case officer for an unrelated attempted murder investigation, which “was of significant priority to ACT Policing”.

As a result, police suspended the investigation into the teens from March to August 2025.

But Magistrate Begley said by making the decision, police risked the integrity of the prosecution.

She pointed out how the majority of the investigation was completed by October 2024.

“The police must have known that they were investigating young people and the decision not to make any meaningful progress in relation to each of the young people for a significant period of time was egregious,” she said.

“It was possible to bring the young people before the court (and therefore to trial) more quickly than they were.”

She found this had been a breach of the teenagers’ human rights.

“If the unlawful conduct of police, in failing to bring the young people to trial, was permitted to continue, there is a significant risk that the rights of young people would be substantially undermined and rendered ineffective,” she said.

Magistrate Begley found continuing the proceedings would involve “an unacceptable injustice” to the teenagers and granted their application for a permanent stay, which brings an end to their prosecution.

A second boy had been represented by the Aboriginal Legal Service (ALS).

Sharif Deen, Acting CEO of ALS NSW/ACT, said the court’s decision confirmed that for children facing criminal charges, delays of this magnitude breach ACT human rights law.

“These delays hang over the heads of children and their families; they make mounting a defence harder when a court date finally arrives, and they delay the benefits of rehabilitative and diversionary sentences,” he said.

Mr Deen said police mistreatment of First Nations people in the ACT and NSW was rampant and there would never be justice for his communities until there was real accountability in the form of independent police oversight.

“But this decision is a step in the right direction,” he said.

“It not only sends a message that police will face accountability when they neglect their duty in relation to children caught in the system, but it also vindicates the ACT’s decision to enact human rights protections into law.”

ACT Human Rights Commissioner Dr Penelope Mathew said the decision highlighted the importance of police and other ACT Government agencies in understanding their obligation to act consistently with human rights, especially when dealing with young people.

“Children in the youth justice system are vulnerable. Authorities must therefore give priority to bringing these matters before the court as quickly as possible.

“When justice agencies breach a person’s human rights there are impacts not just for that person but on the whole justice system – including for victims of crime.”

An ACT Policing spokesperson said the police force had noted the reasons in the decision.

“ACT Policing will consider the findings,” the spokesperson said.

australia.title: Off-grid UK-Australian couple describe ‘anguish’ at removal of children by Italian court
australia.snippet: After judge allows partial access rights, Catherine Birmingham and Nathan Trevallion say the enforced separation ‘broke each of our heart...
australia.content:
A couple have told of their heartache, trauma and stress after fighting for two years for their right to parent their children as they choose in the glare of the world’s attention.

The three children of a Melbourne woman, Catherine Birmingham, and her British partner, Nathan Trevallion, were removed from their “dilapidated” off-grid home in Italy last year.

It sparked global conversations about state intervention and alternative lifestyles.

They were raising the children on a property in the woods in the Abruzzo region, where they grew their own food and homeschooled the children.

In September 2024, the family was hospitalised after eating poisonous mushrooms they had picked, which brought them to the attention of authorities.

In November 2025, the juvenile court ordered the removal of Utopia Rose, nine, and six-year-old twins Galorian and Bluebell to a residential care facility, citing a lack of hygiene, social interaction, toilet facilities and schooling.

Birmingham stayed with them until March, when she was ordered to leave under a new court ruling.

On Wednesday, an Italian court approved a staged process that would allow a “gradual reunification process”, and could eventually allow the children to leave the facility.

“The ruling partially revises previous court decisions and sets out a ‌gradual reunification process, ‌allowing the children to return home for daytime visits immediately and, from October, for weekend ‌overnight stays with their family,” their lawyer, Simone Pillon, said.

In a statement released on Thursday, the couple said the “long-awaited decision, which our entire family awaited with anguish, arrived with a harshness that broke each of our hearts”.

They asked whether forcing school attendance was “fair, legal, and respectful” of their parental rights and the rights of their children, saying they chose Italy for reasons including its homeschooling rights and support for family bonds.

The parents have said that doctors say the children’s health is at “serious risk” and “the only way to reduce this risk is to return them home immediately”.

“We are deeply concerned for their health,” the parents wrote.

“How will they be well if they are forced to travel back and forth from their home to the foster home, then to school, and then back to the foster home again, all while still being kept apart from their parents?

“How will they fare in the evening when, after an afternoon spent at home with their friends and pets, they must return to the foster home?”

Even Italy’s hard-right prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, has weighed in. She expressed “alarm” over the children being taken into care, while the deputy prime minister, Matteo Salvini, compared the case to a kidnapping.

But the judiciary’s union said the court’s decision was based on factors including the children’s safety, sanitary conditions and education.

After the latest decision, social services will monitor the process and make an assessment before any permanent reunion can happen.

The couple wrote that the authorities wanted to impose a standard. “And those who don’t follow it lose their children,” they wrote.

“We are deeply saddened by this.

“We have continued to collaborate and engage with everyone, even under extreme trauma, stress, exasperation and concern for our children knowing their daily suffering but we will always demand respect for our parental rights and, above all, for our children’s rights, especially their right to health – mental, physical and emotional.”

The couple plan to appeal for a complete and faster reunification.

australia.title: Property developer claimed ‘the premier is my best friend’ in tapped phone call, Icac hears
australia.snippet: Charles Perrottet, the younger brother of the former premier, tells Icac that claims made by Jean Nassif in the call were ‘bravado’ and ‘...
australia.content:
A property developer who allegedly made prohibited donations to support factional Liberal work claimed “the premier is my best friend” in a secretly recorded phone call the day after Dominic Perrottet was chosen as New South Wales premier, an inquiry has heard.

Charles Perrottet, the younger brother of the former premier, told the Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) on Thursday that claims made by property developer Jean Nassif in a phone call lawfully intercepted by police were “bravado” and “far-fetched”.

Dominic Perrottet is not named as a person of interest in Icac’s allegations and is not accused of any wrongdoing. Nassif, who fled Australia for Lebanon in 2022, has withdrawn from an expected video appearance on Friday after providing a medical certificate. He has previously denied any wrongdoing.

As part of its inquiry into alleged corruption in the NSW Liberals, Icac is investigating the allegation that conservative factional figures Charles Perrottet, Jeremy Greenwood and Christian Ellis received prohibited donations totalling $2m from Nassif or his company Toplace between 2020 and 2023 in exchange for political outcomes.

The outcomes included damage to the career of former NSW Liberal minister, David Elliott, who had opposed Nassif’s developments, and the removal of former building commissioner, David Chandler, who was scrutinising defects in Toplace apartments.

Ellis is overseas and has not responded to Icac’s allegations, while Greenwood will appear before the commission again next week. Charles Perrottet has repeatedly denied he accepted payments from Nassif in exchange for political outcomes.

On Thursday, the commission heard phone call between Nassif and a friend in which the developer claimed: “The premier is my best friend … They’re my friends and my boys”.

“I only started yesterday. You’re gonna be surprised soon, no jokes, no jokes. I’ve got my hand on the state government, and you’re gonna see changes. You’re gonna see DA approvals for me, like every second week, one DA approved,” he said.

Charles Perrottet, who described a phone conversation between Nassif and his younger brother Jean-Claude Perrottet, in which the developer claimed he had “forced the boys” to get rid of the Liberal branch of Baulkham Hills in Elliott’s seat as “bravado”, said the October 2021 call was “even more far-fetched”.

On Tuesday, the commission heard about a May 2021 meeting between him and Nassif at the Nobu fine-dining restaurant in Melbourne’s Crown Casino. Afterwards, Charles Perrottet wrote he had told the told the developer “the best way to get the building commissioner off his back is to take the fight to Elliott and dismantle his infrastructure”, with the result that Elliott would “be on his knees”.

Referencing the Nobu dinner, counsel assisting, Peggy Dwyer SC, suggested on Thursday it was “little wonder … that Jean Nassif thought that he had the right [faction] in his pocket immediately after your brother got the premiership.”

“I think it’s just bravado. He says he’s the premier’s best friend,” said Charles Perrottet.

The inquiry has previously heard that Charles Perrottet, who texted his wife Anita about a plan to remove Elliott from his ministry once the Perrottet government had formed – writing “we execute the prick once party room is over” – shared a secret phone recording in which Elliott could allegedly be heard criticising Dominic Perrottet.

On Thursday, the commission heard the recording, during which speaking was faintly audible beneath a loud, rhythmic sound, which Dwyer suggested was a “a heartbeat that suggests a recording device”. Charles Perrottet suggested it was a pocket dial, saying he did not recall having the recording until it was mentioned in evidence last week, or how he had obtained it.

The commission heard evidence that he passed it into another NSW Liberal MP and that Ellis shared it with a private investigator employed by Toplace in the hope of improving the audio quality.

‘Charles fucked this whole thing’

Charles Perrottet has previously said he would regularly mislead Nassif, adding a “political flavour” to advice in order to chase up payments for genuine lobbying work by Beckington, a company controlled by Ellis and Greenwood.

On Thursday, the commission heard an exchange sent by Greenwood to Ellis in April 2020, expressing concern about losing Toplace as a client when Nassif’s Cherrybrook development proposal was refused after the Hills shire council did not support it. Charles Perrottet said he did not know what the message – in which Greenwood wrote “Charles fucked this whole thing” – meant.

He was asked about a subsequent exchange between him and Ellis in which he detailed steps to assist with Toplace developments, including a call he wrote he would make to the NSW Liberal MP and former Hills shire councillor Robyn Preston.

On Thursday, Charles Perrottet said he could not recall calling Preston. The counsel assisting, Peggy Dwyer SC, asked if he would “regularly lie to Christian Ellis at that time to tell him you were doing some things and not others?”

“I may have,” said Charles Perrottet, suggesting it might have been “to sound supportive”.

Dwyer, noting he had also said he would lie to Nassif, suggested that “actually the fabrication is the evidence you’re giving to the commission because you want to make it sound like you didn’t take the active steps that are clearly set out in this text”.

“No,” said Charles Perrottet.

Later, he was asked about a message from Greenwood to the Toplace executive Sharangan Maheswaran, also named in Icac’s allegations, in 2021, asking for payment from Nassif, or “Charles is just going to cut the relationship”. After Maheswaran offered to pass on the message, Greenwood expressed concern that Nassif might see it as a threat.

Maheswaran, who is named in a separate allegation, has previously denied any wrongdoing. He will appear before Icac next week.

Under repeated questioning from Dwyer, Charles Perrottet rejected the suggestion it was “clear as day … that Mr Greenwood shared your view, as expressed to Jean Nassif, that he had to hand over the money in order to achieve the political outcomes”.

Icac’s inquiry continues.

    Welcome

What we learned today, Thursday 3 September

That’s where we’ll leave our live coverage for the day.

Before we go, let’s recap the top headlines:

  • The federal government will invest up to $2m in Call It Out – an online register where people can report incidents and experiences of racism and discrimination against First Nations people.

  • Australia will deploy a team of specialist drone operators and commit another a further $3m in aid to help the search and rescue effort in the deadly Nepal-Tibet floods.

  • A teenage boy faced court after a “near-complete amputation” of a boy’s hand during an alleged assault in Sydney on Wednesday night.

  • The Coalition has announced its proposed tobacco policy which would cut the excise rate by 80%. The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, said it would “destroy the business model” of organised crime, but Cancer Council Australia and Quit have warned it threatens to “undermine decades of progress in reducing smoking and preventing cancer”.

  • Financial markets are now pricing in an 80% chance that mortgage holders will get hit with a fourth RBA rate hike at the end of this month, as investors fret that soaring oil prices will reignite inflationary pressures. Meanwhile, officials from the Commonwealth Bank say home loan applications have dropped by about 15% since the May federal budget, when the Albanese government announced a winding back of generous tax breaks for property investors.

  • Australia’s defence minister, Richard Marles, met with his US counterpart, secretary of war Pete Hegseth, at the Pentagon in Washington DC overnight.

  • Ralph Regenvanu, the Vanuatu climate change minister who led a successful case to the international court of justice finding high-emitting countries have a legal duty to stop climate harm, said Australia needs to do more to tackle the warming world.

  • And Sydney will open a new ferry stop at the city’s Walsh Bay arts precinct from next year, which is set to boost accessibility to an area featuring the Sydney Theatre Company, the Sydney Dance Company and Bangarra Dance Company.

Thanks for sticking around, we’ll see you tomorrow!

Woman arrested after 81-year-old man’s body found in creek in northern NSW

A woman has been arrested after police found the body of a man on a property in New South Wales’ Northern Rivers region on Thursday afternoon.

Authorities attended a home near Ballina after responding to reports of concern for a person’s welfare.

Police said they located the body of an 81-year-old man in a creek on the property during a search. The man, who is believed to have lived there, is yet to be formally identified.

A 51-year-old woman was arrested at the home and remains in police custody as investigations continue.

Barnaby Joyce on illicit tobacco: ‘The only way to deal with it is to bring the price of legal cigarettes back into orbit of the illegal ones.’

Continuing his ABC interview, Barnaby Joyce said the current tobacco excise rate was “a complete disaster of a policy” that had only fuelled the illicit market.

The Labor party is sticking to their position that somehow if they start trying to sell packets of cigarettes at $55, and you can go down the street and buy them for $15, magically people are going to start going back to buy their cigarettes. They’re not buying their cigarettes, they’re buying the illegal ones.

The only way to deal with it is to bring the price of legal cigarettes back into orbit of the illegal ones, and then people will pay a premium for a regulated product … both of them will kill you, but at least with the regulated ones you know what is killing you.

Discussing the illicit drug trade, Joyce was asked whether Australia should legalise marijuana and cocaine to combat those black markets. Joyce rejected the premise of the question, adding that tobacco is less dangerous.

If I’m going down the road … what would you rather me doing? Having a bunga in my mouth and smoking it, taking a big long line and sticking it up my nose, or maybe just pulling a whole heap of cones? Which one are you going to feel safer with?

No one has been caught over the limit on cigarettes … if you’re pulling bucket bongs and deciding to go for a drive down to the shops, it’s probably more dangerous.

‘Put out the welcome mat and bring more chairs’: Barnaby Joyce accuses Coalition of copying One Nation’s tobacco policy

Barnaby Joyce has accused the Coalition of “copying One Nation” with its tobacco policy, released days after the minor party announced its own proposal.

The Coalition’s central measure is an 80% cut to the tobacco excise, alongside a $200m law enforcement boost to shut down illegal shops and stop illicit shipments. One Nation has promised to cut tobacco excise by 75%.

Speaking to ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, Joyce said:

It wasn’t a policy before One Nation made it a policy … We should just put out the welcome mat and bring more chairs to the One Nation party room and let’s just get on with it. We can all sit there together.

Maybe we should just email them after we’ve made a decision, just take the dog lead out of this and get policy straight through to the Coalition.

Joyce added that he found the 5% difference between the policies “hilarious”.

I’m glad we didn’t say 90, then they would say 95. We say 100, they would say ‘We’ll pay you to buy cigarettes.’ I don’t want to bucket on the Coalition, but they’re really struggling, aren’t they?

Crisis averted but home developer Bathla still on life support

Administrators for a major housing developer have met a crucial funding deadline, but negotiations to keep the group afloat continue, AAP reports.

Insolvency advisory Teneo has been scrambling to secure $20m in short-term funding for the embattled Bathla Group since it entered voluntary administration in late August.

As administrator, Teneo set a deadline of Thursday to secure the cash injection, which is when payroll for Bathla’s staff fell due.

On Thursday afternoon, Teneo announced it was yet to secure the short-term funding it is seeking from lenders but enough cash had been found to pay wages accrued since August 25.

The partial payment covers the period since Teneo was appointed administrator, but will not meet all wages owed by Bathla, with some staff having not been paid for weeks.

Administrator Stephen Longley said Bathla’s employees had engaged with Teneo constructively, but stressed the payroll target was only the first hurdle.

“The situation is complex,” he said in a statement, adding the short-term funding administrators are still attempting to secure would only afford a few weeks of breathing room.

Teneo will now set its sights on the first formal creditors meeting slated for Friday, where those owed money would engage with administrators, he said.

Andrew Messenger

Opposition claims Queensland government ‘fixed the figures’ after slight dip in crime rate

Queensland’s Labor opposition claims the LNP “fixed the figures” after a slight dip in the state’s reported crime rate in the party’s first year in government.

ABS data released today shows that the number of victims in crime in Queensland declined by about 4% in 2025. It’s broadly in line with the national average and with the rate of decline in Labor’s last year in office, 2024.

The number is politically significant because the premier, David Crisafulli, vowed to resign unless the number of crime victims declined during his first term in office.

The drop is driven by a decline in all assaults, which are down 4%. Burglary also declined about 12%, and motor vehicle theft and other theft victimisation rates have declined by 2%. The number of victims of sexual assault is down 2%, the first decline in the state since 2019. The Labor leader, Steven Miles, said on Thursday:

If you believe these statistics, then domestic violence is down 12% in just a year. I don’t think any of us believe that. What’s changed is how that’s reported.

The shadow minister for women, Shannon Fentiman, said:

This is a government that does not care about domestic and family violence victims, and we see that today in these figures, they have not fixed domestic and family violence. They’ve just fixed the figures.

The government has spent millions in public money claiming its adult crime, adult time laws have reduced crime by more than 9%.

The police minister, Dan Purdie, said the government would continue to increase sentences for some young offenders, in an effort to reduce crime. He said:

Today is a really important day for Queensland. It’s an important day for Queenslanders who have suffered for too long under Labor’s youth crime crisis, and it’s an important day for victims of crime.

‘Nightmare’: Melbourne child dies from infection after petting zoo visit

A three-year-old girl has died after a visit to a petting zoo triggered a bacterial infection, prompting health authorities to raise the alarm about the rare but potentially fatal syndrome, AAP reports.

Sassi died in a Melbourne hospital after developing Haemolytic-uraemic syndrome, known as HUS, seven weeks after a trip to a petting zoo where she held, rode and petted animals, the Salter family said in a GoFundMe post.

The family of four said they had “been living a nightmare” after the toddler spent six weeks in intensive care battling kidney failure and a brain injury. The family wrote:

We’ve lost our darling girl.

Sassi was strong. Surprising many at each corner. She was courageous and a fighter. She fought so hard. We all fought so hard.

The child contracted a strain of the E.Coli bacteria (STEC) which releases toxins into the body, inflaming blood vessels and causing clots which can cause gastro symptoms and damage the kidneys and other organs.

The bacteria is commonly found in the gut of several types of farm animals, including cattle.

The family called on the community to prioritise hand hygiene by carrying hand sanitiser and washing fruit and vegetables.

The STEC bacteria can be passed on to humans by eating undercooked beef, drinking unpasteurised milk, drinking or swimming in contaminated water and contact with farm animals.

About 1,000 STEC infections are reported in Australia each year, of which a very small number of these people develop HUS, the Australian Centre for Disease Control says.

Public health groups warn Coalition’s tobacco and vaping plan could reverse decades of progress in reducing smoking

Cancer Council Australia and Quit have warned that the Coalition’s plans to slash the tobacco excise and legalise vapes threaten to “undermine decades of progress in reducing smoking and preventing cancer”.

Speaking to Channel Nine’s Today program this morning, the deputy opposition leader, Jane Hume, said the plan would “crush the organised crime gangs that are making billions from illegal cigarettes and vapes”. The plan’s central measure is an 80% cut to the tobacco excise, alongside a $200m law enforcement boost to shut down illegal shops and stop illicit shipments.

The anti-smoking organisations warned the proposal could undo “decades of world-leading public health policy” that has helped Australia achieve historically low smoking rates.

Cancer Council Australia’s director of cancer control policy, David Martin, said:

This is not the time to abandon the measures that have delivered those results. The overwhelming majority of cancers caused by smoking are preventable and every policy decision should be judged against one simple question: will it reduce nicotine addiction and smoking, or increase it?

We know that the illicit trade is a serious problem but making tobacco cheaper or creating a commercial vape market will not address it.

Quit medical lead, Dr Liam Egan, added:

Quitline receives calls from young people addicted to vaping and pouches, and struggling to quit. We don’t want to make these harmful, addictive nicotine products easier to access at the very moment we should be doing everything possible to prevent another generation becoming hooked. These proposals go against hard-fought public health wins.

Nick Visser

That’s all from me! Achol Arok will take things from here.

CommBank officials say home loan applications have dropped by 15%

Sarah Basford Canales

Officials from the Commonwealth Bank say home loan applications have dropped by around 15% since the May federal budget when the Albanese government announced a winding back of generous tax breaks for property investors.

Banking managers and economists from the top four banks are appearing at a Senate inquiry into generational housing inequality today.

Robert Parker, CBA’s executive general manager for retail, said there had been a “softening” of lending applications in recent months, with investor loans down about 28% since May, but didn’t have the figure for owner-occupier loans.

Westpac’s head economist, Dr Luci Ellis, said the bank – like other major banks – did not publicly report how much of its $6.9bn profit for 2024-25 was generated from interest on home loans. Ellis said the bank’s consumer division, which includes home mortgages, made $2.3bn in the year, or a third of the overall profit.

Earlier this morning, the Australian Council of Trade Unions assistant secretary, Joseph Mitchell, took aim at the big four banks, describing them as a big factor in housing affordability and ownership in Australia.

There’s not enough competition in the big four banks. Their profitability rates are absolutely enormous. They’re able to charge basically whatever they want for a mortgage because they, [at] the end of the day, are some of the big arbiters about whether or not you get to own a home.

Read more:

Benita Kolovos

Victoria premier commits almost $450m to road projects if re-elected

The Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, held his fourth consecutive press conference regarding the state’s roads this week, announcing $448m to upgrade roads in the western suburbs if re-elected in November.

Carroll announced $195m would go to widening Point Cook Road between Central Avenue and Dunnings Road in Seabrook, $170m to widening Taylors Road in Delahey and Kings Park and $83m to double the capacity at the Ballan Road and Bolton Road intersection in Wyndham Vale.

He told reporters:

Roads, roads and roads are such an important component of what I will do as premier. You don’t need to be a Rhodes scholar to know we need to invest in more roads, fixing potholes, smoother ways home, and getting people home quicker and faster to be with their families.

It’s worth noting each project is in Labor-held electorates that pundits say the party has taken for granted: Kororit, Sydenham, Point Cook and Werribee.

australia.title: Afternoon Update: Coalition tobacco plan lambasted, Queensland coal project approved by new EPA, and EVs v holidays
australia.snippet: Want to get this in your inbox every weekday? Sign up for the Afternoon Update here , and start your day with our Morning Mail newsletter...
australia.content:
Good afternoon.

Leading public health experts, the Australian Medical Association and Labor have rejected Angus Taylor’s plan to cut tobacco excise by 80%, labelling the move to curb soaring illegal cigarette sales as a backward step on tobacco control. 

Under the Coalition’s plan, the excise on a standard packet of 20 cigarettes would be cut from about $30 to about $6, while moves would be made to legalise and regulate vapes and nicotine pouches. The opposition leader argues the changes would undermine illicit tobacco dealers, who currently control more than half of all sales in Australia.

The Australian Medical Association president, Danielle McMullen, said the Coalition’s plan would undermine decades of public health efforts, while the Labor frontbencher Tanya Plibersek said the Coalition’s plan “will kill people”.

Top news

  • Chilling footage shows Molly Ticehurst’s murderer saying ‘I can’t believe I just did that’, court hears

  • Dutch central bank moves 86 tonnes of gold to UK from US and Canada, citing ‘geopolitical unrest’

  • Six-year-old boy died from scurvy despite long-term concerns over diet, Queensland coroner finds

  • Gang violence is not ‘out of control’ in Sydney, police minister says after two shootings in two days

  • The place that never freezes: the Arctic habitat where global heating threatens more ice, not less

In video

What they said …

“The very least a country like Australia should be doing is stopping future expansion, and it’s not doing that.” – Vanuatu climate minister Ralph Regenvanu

Australia’s new national agency for environmental protection has approved its first coal project, allowing a Queensland open-cut mine to keep digging until 2055 while clearing threatened woodland and koala habitat.

Ralph Regenvanu, the Vanuatu climate change minister who led a successful case to the international court of justice finding high-emitting countries have a legal duty to stop climate harm, said Australia needs to do more to tackle the warming world. “This means a rapid transitioning away from fossil fuels and fossil fuel subsidies. There’s no other way,” he said.

When asked about fossil fuel expansions, Anthony Albanese denied that leaders of Pacific nations who fear for their country’s future because of rising sea levels had raised objections. “No, they don’t do that,” he said, “The Pacific leaders have respect for the position that we’ve taken.”

Podcast

Guardian Essential report: does One Nation have a fix for social isolation? – Australian Politics podcast

One Nation has had another electoral win, having flipped the Labor seat of Secret Harbour in a Western Australian byelection on Saturday. So what does this signal for the upcoming contest at the Victorian state election?

Guardian Australia political reporter Krishani Dhanji speaks with Essential executive director Peter Lewis about how Pauline Hanson’s party is tapping into low social engagement, and how Labor can better respond during this time of technological and global uncertainty.

Listen to the episode here.

Before bed read

Australians are buying EVs instead of holidaying in Europe. Economics editor Patrick Commins brings you the key takeaways from the latest national accounts from the Australian Bureau of Statistics.

Daily word game

Today’s starter word is: COOK. You have five goes to get the longest word including the starter word. Play Wordiply.

Sign up

australia.title: Who are the Australians missing in the Nepal floods? What we know so far
australia.snippet: There are 38 Australians among the thousands of people missing as rescue efforts continue after deadly flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet bo...
australia.content:
The number of Australians missing in the Nepal-Tibet flash flooding disaster fell from 43 on Tuesday morning to 38 on Wednesday, with five unaccounted for people making contact.

Of the five Australians confirmed safe on Wednesday, one was found in Nepal, one in Tibet and three outside the crisis-hit area.

It comes after Sydney woman Cara Severino, 25, was safely located in Nepal last week.

The names of the five Australians confirmed safe on Wednesday have not yet been released.

Pilgrims trekking to a holy site in Tibet make up the majority of Australians who have been reported missing after deadly flash floods and landslides tore through valleys on the Nepal-Tibet border on 26 August. Most were travelling with Himalayan Glacier Adventures, Kailash Journeys and the Isha Foundation.

Across Nepal and Tibet, more than 4,000 people have been reported missing and Nepali and Chinese authorities have confirmed more than 1,000 have died.

Here’s what we know about the Australians who remain missing. This article will be updated as more information becomes available.

Venkatraman Balakrishnan and Chitra Venkatraman

New South Wales couple Venkatraman Balakrishnan, 52, and Chitra Venkatraman, 46, were among 15 Australians travelling to Mount Kailash on a spiritual trip with the Himalayan Glacier Adventures tour group.

Their son, Akash Venkatraman, said his parents had planned to leave their riverside accommodation in Syabrubesi before it was devastated by flood waters.

Muralitharan family

Shylaja Muralitharan, 42, Chandresekaran Muralitharan, 47 and their children Ashwin, 14, and Aarush, 11, were also taking part in the Himalayan Glacier Adventures spiritual tour to Mount Kailash when the flood hit.

The parents and two children had been training together for the long walk, Shylaja’s younger sister Vaishnavi said.

She lost contact with the family shortly after their breakfast on the morning of the flood.

Iyer family

Sreedharan Iyer, 52, and Lakshmi Iyer, 50, and their adult sons Rishab Iyer, 23, and Rudhra Iyer, 20, were taking part in the spiritual pilgrimage to Mount Kailash with Himalayan Glacier Adventures.

The Iyer brothers are medical students at the University of Newcastle and members of the West Pennant Hills Cherrybrook Cricket Club in Sydney’s north-west.

Karan Bhardwaj, Arpan Mithalal Kothari and Bhavin Raval

Karan Bhardwaj, Arpan Mithalal Kothari and Bhavin Raval were travelling together on a Kailash Journey tour of the region. Bhardwaj’s family says the three men have known each other since 2009, when they met at university.

Raval’s wife, Bhavinkumar Raval, has told the ABC she believes her husband is still alive and is making plans to travel to Nepal.

Bhardwaj is a 40-year-old Brisbane-based member of the Royal Australian Air Force.

Bhardwaj’s family member Jen said: “Karan is a dad to my beautiful seven-year-old nephew, as well as a brother, uncle and brother in law. He is so desperately loved by his family and right now we are desperately praying, hoping and believing that Karan is safe, alive and somehow making his way back to us.”

Narayan Panthi

Narayan Panthi, from Brisbane, has been listed by Nepali police as travelling with operator Kathmandu Holiday Tours and Travel. It is understood Panthi had been carrying out independent volunteer charity work in Kathmandu earlier in the week before travelling towards the border region.

Panthi’s cousin, Amrit Bhusal, told Guardian Australia his family were devastated but “holding on to hope and praying for positive news”.

“We are still hoping,” Bhusal said. “We are still searching. We are still praying for Narayan to come home safely.”

Bhusal said Panthi had been “helping disadvantaged children in Nepal reach their full potential through education”.

Bharat Mangwani

Bharat Mangwani, 42, was travelling with the Isha Foundation as part of a pilgrimage to Lake Manasarovar when his family lost contact with him on Wednesday morning.

He was last seen at Gyirong before the group was set to depart for Kathmandu.

“All of us are praying for him and hopefully he comes back to us soon,” close friend Kushagra Tiwari said.

Mangwani’s family, including his nine-year-old son and three-year-old daughter, have travelled to India with a family friend, while his wife has flown to Nepal to look for him.

Sumi Adhikari

Sumi Adhikari, 41, was at the Gyirong Port crossing with the Isha Foundation group when the flood hit.

Her husband, Nava Pandey, has travelled to Nepal seeking information about her whereabouts.

“We still have no clear or official information about Sumi or the other members of her group,” Pandey said on Saturday morning.

Renee Spry

A Sunshine Coast disability support worker, Renee Spry has been described as a “deeply spiritual” person who travelled to Nepal on a pilgrimage.

“She had two degrees, and she chose to do something that was … a completely selfless vocation. Her priority was always other people,” her sister Clair Spry said.

“Every person she touched, they knew her love and kindness. She would be so uncomfortable with all this.”

Clair Spry has set up a GoFundMe so her family can travel to Nepal to look for signs of Renee.

Suhasini Kandimalla

A mother of two from Springfield, near Brisbane, Suhasini Kandimalla was hiking with another Springfield local, according to her sister, Supreethini Kandimalla.

While she was a New Zealand citizen, Suhasini had been approved for Australian citizenship, her sister said. She had planned to attend a citizenship ceremony for it to be granted soon after she returned.

“I don’t know if it was a religious calling for her to do it,” Supreethini said of the Nepal trip.

“But she certainly loved the treks in New Zealand too, and would go on lots of long hikes.”

Reshma Patel

Newcastle woman Reshma Patel, 46, was in the Isha Foundation group. She didn’t know Sumi Adhikari beforehand, but the pair had become friends on the pilgrimage, Patel’s family friend Chin Valsan says.

“They were talking to each other, and they were supposed to come back on the same flight on Thursday,” he says.

He describes Patel, who has two children aged 10 and 14 and works casually for Canterbury-Bankstown council, as “full of life” and a “kind soul” who loves her family and friends.

Kanagamah Sundrasan

The mother of two from Springfield, near Brisbane, was part of the Kailash Journey trek to Mount Kailash.

Her daughter, Swaatika Kanniah, said her mother had been excited about the hike.

“It was a pilgrimage, she really wanted to go and have that experience.”

A photograph of her on the trip shows her smiling with five other members of the tour; all are now missing.

“I feel like everyone is trying their best, but yes we don’t know much about what’s going on,” Kanniah said of the recovery efforts.

Michael Keats

The family of 37-year-old Michael Keats, from Mollymook in NSW, said on social media that he had died.

Keats’s partner, Emily Boyd, said on Instagram on Sunday that he had been on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, which had been his “dream for many years”.

“Mike went on a pilgrimage to Mt Kailash seeking enlightenment,” Boyd said.

“There’s a bittersweetness knowing that there was nothing more that Mike wanted [than] to know God, and to merge with the divine.

“He was a mystic, a medicine man, a teacher, leader, partner, father, brother, son, uncle and dearly beloved friend. He showed up for so many people in so many ways. A heart of pure gold. We love you forever and always.”

On Tuesday, the foreign minister, Penny Wong, said the Australian government “has not yet received official confirmation of Mr Keats’ passing. He does remain unaccounted for in terms of the information we have. But … we respect the rights of the families to make the statements they have”.

“Our thoughts go out to his family and to every Australian family who is hoping that the many who are missing can be located,” she said.

Luke Costanzo

Luke Costanzo, 30, from Perth remains missing, his family has confirmed.

He was on a pilgrimage trek with the Isha foundation, and the group was last in contact at the Gyirong port border crossing as they were making their way back to Kathmandu on the final day of their journey, the family said in a statement.

“Luke is an extremely strong, compassionate, disciplined and spiritual person. Once he makes a decision he commits to it fully and he was so excited to be visiting Mount Kailash on a pilgrimage trek with the Isha Foundation,” the family said.

“We truly appreciate all the love and support from friends and family that we’ve received and ask everyone to keep Luke, and all those affected, in your thoughts and prayers.”

The family has asked people who wish to help to donate “to aid the wonderful people on the ground who continue with rescue efforts”.

Sandeep Mohapatra and Sidharthi Kumari Sahu

Sandeep Mohapatra and Sidharthi Kumari Sahu are members of Melbourne’s Odia community.

The couple had taken part in a pilgrimage and were last believed to have been making their way towards the immigration office.

Hara Patro, a member of the Melbourne Odia community, travelled to India to speak with their families and has urged Australians to keep the couple in their hearts.

“Their families are living through unimaginable uncertainty,” he said.

“Every day without news makes the situation harder, but we continue to hope and pray that Sandeep and Sidharthi will be found safe.”

The couple’s son is staying with family in India as they wait for news.

world.title: Victims sue South African government over 1961 Sharpeville massacre that left 91 dead
world.snippet: Claim relating to infamous apartheid-era shooting of protesters part of wave of litigation for apartheid-era crimes The day dawned bright...
world.content:
The day dawned brightly on 21 March 1960, as residents of the South African township of Sharpeville gathered to protest against pass laws, which forced “Black, Indian and Coloured” South Africans to carry documents at all times specifying where they were allowed to be.

Abraham Mofokeng joined the march, one of dozens organised nationwide by the Pan Africanist Congress (PAC), a breakaway group from the African National Congress (ANC). “The weather was very nice, the sun was out. You could not have suspected that the day would go so horribly,” said Mofokeng, who was then a 20-year-old factory worker.

Mofokeng, now 86, was among the thousands gathered peacefully outside the police station in Sharpeville, which is about 40 miles south of Johannesburg in a heavily industrialised region known as the Vaal Triangle.

The crowd was singing, he said, when officers opened fire without warning. At least 91 people were killed and 238 injured, in what became known as the Sharpeville massacre.

As Mofokeng fled, a bullet grazed the inside of his right foot, ripping his shoe off. A woman fell to the ground before him; he jumped over her and kept running. Only later, when he noticed blood running down his legs, did he realise he had been shot in the back, where a bullet remains lodged in his spine.

Mofokeng is among three claimants suing the South African government, in a case filed on Thursday, for compensation for the massacre. If the case is successful, dozens more could file claims.

The case is part of a wave of litigation demanding justice for apartheid-era crimes, amid widespread disillusionment with ANC-led governments that have failed to rectify South Africa’s huge racial inequality and poverty since the end of apartheid over three decades ago.

In January 2025, 25 survivors and relatives of victims of apartheid state violence sued South Africa’s government for failing to prosecute cases referred to it by the post-apartheid Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC). That May, the president, Cyril Ramaphosa, announced a judicial inquiry into potential political interference, which is still ongoing.

Spokespeople for South Africa’s justice department did not respond to a request for comment on the Sharpeville compensation case.

In the immediate aftermath of the Sharpeville massacre, police claimed protesters had been throwing rocks at them. “I don’t know how many we shot,” said Col J Pienaar, the local police commander, according to a story published by the Guardian the following day. “It all started when hordes of natives surrounded the police station. My car was struck with a stone. If they do these things they must learn their lesson the hard way.”

In July 1961, in response to victims filing compensation claims, the white minority regime passed a law indemnifying the government and anyone acting under its authority for any actions taken “in good faith for the prevention or suppression of internal disorder, the maintenance or restoration of good order, public safety or essential services, or the preservation of life or property”.

The law, which was made effective retrospectively from the date of the massacre, is still in force today. The claimants’ legal team is arguing that the law is unconstitutional.

The claimants are hoping to get compensation of about 500,000 rand (£23,000), said Daniel Leader, a partner with the UK law firm Leigh Day, which is advising the South African legal team, led by Lawyers For Human Rights, an NGO.

Mafokeng was awarded 30,000 rand as a one-off payment, after the TRC concluded in 2003. The TRC had recommended annual reparations payments of about 20,000 rand for six years.

“We continued to suffer,” said Mofokeng, who still lives in Sharpeville. “Especially now … I am struggling and my health is not up to standard.”

The other two test claimants were children when their fathers were killed in the massacre. Paulina Mathinye was five when her father, Samson, was shot. “Every time he came back from work, I would be so happy to see him that I would run to him, and then he would pick me up,” she said.

Mathinye did not initially understand what had happened that day in 1960. “I kept on asking my mum: ‘Mummy, why are you crying?’”

Mathinye’s mother struggled to raise her five children on a domestic worker’s wages and Mathinye, who had wanted to train as a teacher but could not afford the bursary, had to leave education at 17 to find work.

Mathinye, who is now 71, said she hoped for compensation that would make up for some of what she lost when her father died. “Some of my friends are teachers, some of them are nurses, and I’m staying in the same house that my father did,” she said.

Sharpeville’s problems did not begin with the massacre in 1960, but with the dispossession of Black South Africans from productive land, their forced removals to townships and their exclusion from the economy, said Vincent Thamae, a PAC member who supports the massacre victims and their families.

“When people talk about compensation now,” he said, “compensation is a concept to them that includes all the land that they lost, the economy that they were taken out of and even how they have been treated in the new democracy.”

world.title: New constitution in Guinea-Bissau will undermine democracy, opponents say
world.snippet: Referendum result means fewer seats in parliament and new rules on candidates, ahead of December elections Guinea-Bissau voters have appr...
world.content:
Guinea-Bissau voters have approved a new constitution, which critics say will undermine democracy, that significantly expands presidential powers ahead of elections due in December.

According to provisional results, 70% of voters approved sweeping changes in the tiny west African state’s first constitutional amendment since revisions that ended the one-party socialist state more than three decades ago.

The turnout for Sunday’s referendum was reportedly over 55%, amounting to an estimated 544,060 people.

The new constitution will reduce the number of seats in parliament from 102 to 65 and cut electoral constituencies from 29 to 12. New provisions will require presidential candidates to have lived continuously in the country for at least five years before the vote, which is believed to target diaspora-based politicians with significant followings.

The referendum’s outcome is expected to pave the way for December’s elections, which many hope will steady the political landscape in Guinea-Bissau, which has been through a series of politically turbulent periods since its declaration of independence from Portugal was globally recognised in 1974. Since then it has had at least 10 coup attempts, half of which have been successful.

The most recent came after last November’s disputed presidential elections. Both candidates declared themselves winners, citing electoral malpractice by the other’s camp. The military forcefully intervened, setting up a transitional ruling council headed by Gen Horta Inta-A Na Man, a former military chief of general staff.

Na Man said: “What we want after this referendum is to allow whoever wins the elections to see out their mandate without hindrance.”

Nelson Moreira, the second vice-president of the transitional council, said the outgoing constitution, which came into effect in 1993, had often been cited as “the cause of instability in Guinea”.

The leading opposition party, the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde (PAIGC), which was barred from fielding a presidential candidate in the 2025 election, had asked its supporters to boycott the referendum, which it called a democratic farce.

“What will happen on 30 August is the continuation of the coup d’état carried out on 26 November,” its leader, Domingos Simões Pereira, had said.

world.title: Almost half of world’s farmers poisoned by pesticides every year, experts find
world.snippet: Study reveals that pesticide poisoning kills 11,000 people each year, with India accounting for nearly 60% of fatalities Almost half of t...
world.content:
Almost half of the world’s farmers are poisoned by pesticides every single year, a study has found.

Using publicly available data from 2006-2023, the study, which was commissioned by Pesticide Action Network, found there to be an estimated 402-433m cases of unintentional acute pesticide poisoning of farmers and farm workers every year.

Based on a worldwide farming population of 934 million, this means approximately 46% of farmers are being poisoned every year. The greatest estimated number of poisonings was in southern Asia, followed by south-east Asia and east Africa.

The overall highest national incidence of poisoning was in Burkina Faso in west Africa, where nearly 84% of farmers and farm workers were reported to have experienced poisoning.

The study, published in the journal Frontiers in Public Health on Wednesday, also found that an estimated 11,000 deaths occur every year due to pesticide poisoning, with nearly 60% of these in India.

Jayakumar Chelaton, the executive director of Pesticide Action Network India, said the research exposed a “crisis that can no longer be ignored”.

The authors of the study are calling for “immediate action”, including the implementation of a UN recommendation to phase out highly hazardous pesticides.

The study states that despite global efforts to highlight the dangers, pesticide use has continued to grow steadily, with 3.8m tonnes used in 2023, a doubling since 1990.

Dr Sheila Willis, the head of international programmes at Pesticide Action Network UK, said: “Now that the scale of suffering has been revealed, farmers must be supported to access safer alternatives to protect their health and that of their families.”

The study did not consider the impact of pesticide exposure on the estimated 84 million children working in agriculture and did not look at the long-term health impacts, with acute pesticide poisoning defined in the study as any illness or health effect experienced a short time after exposure.

Génon Jensen, the executive director of the Health and Environment Alliance, said: “We are extremely concerned about the devastating health impacts from pesticide poisonings – both the acute impacts mentioned in this study but also chronic exposures that farm workers and communities suffer.”

Hélène Nicora, the director general of Parkinson’s Europe, said there was also “overwhelming evidence” to suggest that Parkinson’s was an environmentally driven disease, with growing evidence linking pesticide exposure to the development of Parkinson’s.

Parkinson’s disease is a progressive disorder in which parts of the brain become damaged over time, affecting movement and balance. The global burden of the disease is rising, with France, Germany and Italy all recognising it as an occupational disease for farmers.

Farmers and farm workers are mainly exposed to pesticides during preparation and application, as well as when touching treated crops and contaminated equipment or clothing.

Speaking at a webinar organised by Friends of the Earth Europe earlier this year, Rendert Algra said he believed his Parkinson’s disease was linked to the pesticides he had used when working at his family farm in the Netherlands.

“Being the eldest son, I did all the spraying of pesticides in our fields for several years in a row,” he said.

Despite being the most robust study to date, the report highlights that available information on pesticide poisoning is inadequate, with the authors calling for standardised surveillance and reporting protocols so that pesticide-related poisonings become reliable and comparable.

world.title: South African airline defends dramatic low-level flyby before rugby union clash
world.snippet: Cape Town stunt sparks major debate over safety risks Airlink insists flyby conducted according to regulations A pre-game stunt involving...
world.content:
A pre-game stunt involving two passenger jets flying dramatically low over a stadium in South Africa drew huge cheers from the estimated crowd of 56,000 people, but also sparked a major debate over safety risks. The flyby by two Embraer jets, operated by the local airline Airlink, happened on Saturday before the second rugby union Test between South Africa and New Zealand in Cape Town.

The flight tracking service Flightradar24 estimated that the lead jet passed just 41-46 feet (12-14 metres) above the roof of Cape Town Stadium, with the crowd and the world’s top-ranked rugby teams below. The second jet, which was very close behind, flew through a cloud of pink dust that shot up from the stadium roof as part of the show.

Airlink, a sponsor of the South Africa rugby union team, said the flyby was conducted according to safety regulations. The airline said that it was carefully planned and rehearsed, with the aircraft flying at 150 knots (172 mph), when they went over the stadium. Each jet had three senior captains on board, Airlink said, operating in the roles of a commander, a co-pilot and a safety officer. The jets were not carrying any passengers.

“Airlink notes the concerns expressed in various social media and online forums regarding yesterday’s formation flyby over Cape Town’s DHL Stadium,” Airlink said on Sunday. “The flight demanded careful planning and rehearsal, as it required navigating at low altitude, at around 150 knots. The South African Civil Aviation Authority and Air Traffic Navigation Services provided valuable guidance, approval and support to ensure a safe flyby.”

South African rugby union has a tradition of stadium flybys at big games, starting when a Boeing 747 flew over a stadium in Johannesburg before the 1995 World Cup final between the same teams, who are fierce rivals. But the flyby last weekend was especially low and dramatic, generating global interest after it was shown as part of the pre-game broadcast, and sparking a flurry of videos shot by witnesses.

Some aviation experts questioned whether the margin for error was too small. “Basically, that lead aircraft … was kind of like dodging over the roof and climbing over the one side and dipping below and then climbing over the other side. That was a little bit uncomfortable,” Chris Martinus, president of Aircraft Owners and Pilots Association South Africa, said. “[If] something adverse happens, you just don’t have options at that kind of altitude.”

Keith Tonkin, an Australian aviation consultant and former military and commercial pilot, said yesteron Monday that the Embraer passenger jets – which are small-to-medium jets designed for regional flights – were not designed or intended for that kind of low-level operation and warned against the precedent.

“The bigger picture is that a benchmark has been established and others may expect to do something similar, and that’s not going to end well,” Tonkin said. He added that turbulence or a bird strike at such a low altitude could leave the pilots with too little room to manoeuvre without hitting the stadium.Airlink said flight data recorded by both aircraft confirmed their flights were performed within civil aviation safety limits for speed and altitude.

world.title: Countries legally obliged to consider slavery reparations, says UN committee
world.snippet: Guidance says states must implement ‘comprehensive measures’ to address legacy of racial discrimination A UN committee has said countries...
world.content:
A UN committee has said countries are legally obliged to consider reparations for the transatlantic slave trade and take other ⁠measures to address the enduring ⁠legacy of racial ​discrimination.

Guidance published on Monday by the committee on the elimination of racial discrimination (CERD) said the obligations arose from ⁠a legally binding 1965 convention on racial discrimination, not from the legal standards that existed when the slave trade took place.

The committee described the approach as a “paradigm ⁠shift” away from debates over historical responsibility that have often been used by governments to resist reparations ​claims.

“States parties must implement comprehensive reparatory measures for ‌people of African descent, ‌covering all aspects of remedies,” said the UN document, which may be cited in courtrooms.

At least 12.5 ‌million Africans were taken and sold between the 15th and 19th centuries in what CERD called the largest forced displacement in history.

Calls for reparations – ranging from official apologies to financial compensation – have gained momentum internationally, though opponents argue states and institutions should not be held responsible for historical crimes. The EU and Britain abstained from a UN resolution ‌on slavery in March.

Some states have sought to dodge claims for justice in courtrooms by arguing that there were no international laws outlawing the slave trade ​at the time – the so-called intertemporality principle.

But the UN document argues that, regardless of whether slavery and the slave trade were illegal under the laws of the day, countries remain responsible under current international obligations to tackle their continuing effects.

“Irrespective of the legal characterisation of the original historical acts, states parties remain bound ⁠by their present obligations under the convention to address structural inequalities,” the UN document ​says.

Financial compensation alone is ​not sufficient, it adds, urging “transformative” measures including ​opening archives, revising public memorials and establishing independent truth commissions.

Pela Boker Wilson, a committee expert ​from Liberia who helped draft ‌the document, said ​she expected states ​to move beyond broad expressions of regret and review policies and laws.

“We are calling on state parties to take concrete and meaningful action,” she told Reuters. “We want to affirm the dignity of those whose suffering was denied, whose suffering was minimised or forgotten.”
